description: How convergence and cross-platform ownership have reshaped the media landscape audiences navigate.
content_html:
What Is Convergence?

Twenty years ago, television was watched on a television set, music was purchased on physical media and the internet was accessed via a desktop computer. Today a single smartphone can do all of these things — and a single global platform might deliver all three simultaneously. This blurring of previously distinct technologies, industries and platforms is what media theorists call convergence.

Convergence operates at several levels. At the technological level, different devices can now perform the same functions — a television set, a tablet, a laptop and a phone can all stream the same film. At the industrial level, companies that once operated in a single sector (say, a telephone network) now operate across content, distribution and platform simultaneously. At the cultural level, audiences engage with content across multiple touchpoints — watching a series, discussing it on social media, playing a related video game and buying related merchandise, often from the same parent conglomerate.

Key Fact

The specification identifies three types of provider whose convergence has reshaped the media landscape: content providers (who make media products), network providers (who transmit them) and platform providers (who deliver them to audiences). Where these were once separate industries, they are now frequently integrated within a single organisation.

Henry Jenkins and Convergence Culture

The theorist Henry Jenkins offered one of the most influential frameworks for understanding convergence. Jenkins argued that convergence is not simply a technological shift — it is a cultural one. He described a world in which “old and new media collide” and in which audiences move actively across platforms rather than sitting passively in front of a single screen.

A key concept from Jenkins is transmedia storytelling — a practice in which a single narrative universe extends across films, television series, video games, comic books, social media and other platforms. Each platform adds something unique; the full story only becomes visible to an audience member who engages across multiple forms. This is now a standard industrial strategy for major media franchises, not merely a creative experiment.

Cross-media ownership describes the situation in which a single organisation controls media products across multiple forms simultaneously. This differs from simple horizontal integration (owning several of the same type of company) because cross-media ownership spans forms — the same owner might control a newspaper, a television channel, a streaming platform and a social media property.

At its most complete, cross-media ownership creates what analysts describe as a “vertical stack”: an organisation that creates content, owns the network that transmits it and controls the platform through which audiences access it. This gives the organisation extraordinary leverage — it can favour its own content, control the terms on which competitors access the platform and collect audience data at every stage of the relationship.

The Second Screen and Platform Integration

Convergence is not only an industrial phenomenon — it shapes how audiences actually behave. Research consistently shows that many viewers watch television while simultaneously using a smartphone or tablet to discuss, search or react to what they are watching. This is sometimes called second-screen viewing. Media organisations have responded to this behaviour by designing content and marketing campaigns that actively invite second-screen participation — using hashtags, live polls and social media tie-ins to extend the audience’s engagement beyond the primary screen.

Key Fact

Jenkins argued that convergence changes not only the technology through which audiences receive media but also the cultural practices through which they engage with it. Audiences become active participants, moving across platforms and generating their own responses — rather than passively receiving a fixed product on a single device.

Convergence has accelerated the globalisation of the media landscape. A subscription streaming service based in one country can reach subscribers in over 150 countries simultaneously, bypassing the national distribution infrastructure that once made global media expansion slow and expensive. This has created intense competition among major platform providers — sometimes described as the “streaming wars” — in which organisations compete for subscriber numbers, exclusive content and talent.

The consequences for smaller national media industries are significant. When global platforms dominate the market in a given country, they can overshadow local broadcasters and independent producers. They also shape what kinds of content are commissioned — content with broad international appeal is privileged over regionally specific stories that might have strong local relevance but limited global market value. This tension between convergence-driven globalisation and national or regional media identity is a recurring theme in the Media Industries framework.
exam_tip_html: When applying Jenkins’ convergence theory in an extended response, do not simply say “convergence means everything is on one device.” The strongest answers distinguish between technological convergence (devices and platforms merging) and cultural convergence (audiences engaging across platforms as active participants), then show how a specific media product or industry illustrates both dimensions. Examiners reward the distinction between the two levels of convergence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Convergence describes the merging of previously separate technologies, platforms and industries; the specification distinguishes content providers, network providers and platform providers whose convergence has reshaped the media landscape.
  • Henry Jenkins argued that convergence is a cultural shift as much as a technological one: audiences move actively across platforms through transmedia storytelling rather than passively receiving a single product.
  • Cross-media ownership and global streaming platforms have intensified convergence at the industrial level, creating tension between globally dominant platforms and locally specific national or regional media.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist argued that convergence is a cultural shift as well as a technological one, describing it as a world in which old and new media collide?
practice_questions.marks: Henry Jenkins. Distractor check: Stuart Hall = encoding/decoding, representation theory; Curran and Seaton = ownership and power; David Hesmondhalgh = cultural industries.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which convergence has changed the way audiences engage with media products.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid example: second-screen viewing, engaging with transmedia storytelling across platforms, discussing content on social media while watching, accessing the same content across multiple devices.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain what is meant by 'transmedia storytelling'.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying transmedia storytelling (a story that unfolds across multiple platforms). One mark for explaining how it works, e.g. each platform (film, game, social media, comic) adds something unique to the narrative, so the audience must engage across several forms to experience the full story.

practice_questions.text: Explain what cross-media ownership means and why it gives a conglomerate significant power in the media landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition of cross-media ownership; clear and developed analysis of the power it generates through control of content, distribution network and platform simultaneously; reference to data collection or terms-of-access leverage.
Secure: Accurate definition; some explanation of the power advantage; limited analytical depth.
Developing: Basic definition; power advantage acknowledged but not well explained.
Emerging: Vague or partial definition; reasons for power advantage missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the convergence of content, network and platform providers has changed the media landscape, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of how convergence brings together previously separate industry roles; specific and well-developed example showing all three provider types integrated in one organisation; analytical link between convergence and consequences for audiences or competitors.
Secure: Accurate explanation of convergence; relevant example; link to consequences made.
Developing: Some explanation; example present but underdeveloped or weakly integrated.
Emerging: Basic or confused account of convergence; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Using Henry Jenkins' ideas about convergence culture, analyse how a media product you have studied uses multiple platforms to engage its audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, accurate application of Jenkins' convergence theory, distinguishing technological and cultural dimensions; detailed analysis of how a specific studied product extends across platforms; specific examples of how each platform contributes differently to the audience experience; acknowledgement of the limits or counter-arguments to Jenkins' optimistic view of active audiences.
Secure: Accurate reference to Jenkins; clear argument about cross-platform engagement; relevant product examples; some analytical depth.
Developing: Jenkins named but theory not fully applied; product referenced but mainly descriptive; cross-platform argument limited.
Emerging: Jenkins mentioned vaguely or misattributed; mainly descriptive; product examples absent or underdeveloped.

knowledge_checks.q: What does Henry Jenkins mean when he describes convergence as a 'cultural shift'?
options: That streaming services have replaced broadcast television
That audiences now engage actively across multiple platforms rather than passively receiving one product
That all media forms are owned by a single company
That technology has made media products cheaper to produce

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes storytelling that unfolds across multiple platforms, with each one adding something unique to the narrative?
Using a smartphone or tablet to discuss or search for content while simultaneously watching television is known as _____ viewing.
When a single organisation controls media across different forms such as television, newspapers and streaming services, this is called _____ ownership.
Match each provider type to its role in the converged media landscape.
right: Creates the media products audiences consume

flashcard_questions.q: What is convergence in the media industries?
flashcard_questions.a: The coming together of previously separate technologies, platforms and industries into integrated systems.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Henry Jenkins' key argument about convergence?
flashcard_questions.a: Convergence is a cultural shift as well as a technological one; audiences engage actively across platforms.
A narrative that extends across multiple platforms, with each medium making a distinct contribution.
When one organisation controls media across multiple forms such as TV, newspapers and streaming.
Using a smartphone or tablet alongside a television to discuss or search related content.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'vertical stack' in media ownership?
flashcard_questions.a: An organisation that creates content, owns the transmission network and controls the delivery platform.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three provider types identified in the spec?
flashcard_questions.a: Content provider, network provider and platform provider.

flashcard_questions.q: How has convergence affected national media industries?
flashcard_questions.a: Global platforms can overshadow local broadcasters and favour content with international rather than local appeal.
Intense competition among major streaming platforms for subscribers, exclusive content and talent.

glossary_terms.definition: The coming together of previously separate technologies, platforms, industries or media forms into integrated systems.
A media scholar who argued that convergence is as much a cultural shift in how audiences engage with content as it is a technological change in how content is delivered.
Storytelling that unfolds across multiple platforms, with each medium making a distinct contribution to the overall narrative world.
When a single company owns media organisations across different forms and platforms, such as a conglomerate controlling television, newspapers, film studios and streaming services.
The use of a smartphone, tablet or laptop alongside a primary television screen, typically for related social media activity, searching or interaction.

hero_image_caption: Multiple connected screens showing how convergence unites previously separate media platforms.
